title: Coastline Ruler Lesson
plainSentence: A lesson that lets you measure a coastline with shorter and shorter rulers, watch its length keep growing, then read off how wiggly it is.
pitch: You walk a ruler along a wiggly coast, shrink it, and see the length climb instead of settling, while a circle quietly settles to a fixed answer. A live chart of ruler size against measured length turns the climb into a straight line whose steepness is the coast's roughness (its fractal dimension), and you finish by ranking mystery coasts by eye and checking yourself.
firstMinute: The first frame shows a jagged coast with a ruler already walking along it in steps, a length readout, and a slider labelled 'ruler size'. Dragging the slider down makes the ruler re-walk the coast and the length number climb, with a second panel beside it where a smooth circle barely changes. First success: the visitor sees the same coast give 2,800 then 3,400 style jumps just by changing the ruler.
conceptsToLearn: Length can be estimated by counting how many equal ruler steps it takes to walk along a curve
whyNow: Timeless and very visual: it makes the coastline paradox a thing you do rather than a fact you read, and ends on a number (roughness) the visitor can measure themselves. It is a geometry lesson, not number theory, so it sits apart from the other maths candidates this round.

purposeDetail.concept: A wiggly curve such as a coastline has no single length: the measured length depends on the ruler. For a curve with fractal dimension D between 1 and 2, the measured length grows roughly like (ruler size) raised to the power (1 minus D) as the ruler shrinks, so a log-log plot of length against ruler size is close to a straight line with slope 1 minus D. A smooth curve has D = 1 and its length settles; the Koch curve has D = ln 4 / ln 3, about 1.26.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: The coastline paradox is usually quoted as a fun fact and stops there. Few explanations let the learner do the measuring, see why the line on the log-log plot appears, and use its slope to get a number.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious adults and students aged about 14 and up, teachers, and anyone who has met 'fractals' as pretty pictures only.
misconceptions: A coastline has one true length that a good enough measurement would find
Smaller rulers just give a more accurate number of the same quantity, so the length must level off for every curve
Dimension has to be a whole number
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: On the log-log chart the points for the Koch coast fall on a straight line while the circle's line is flat, and the steepness of the coast's line is exactly the extra wiggliness the ruler keeps discovering.
demos: Rung 1: walk a ruler along a gentle curve and a circle; the length settles as the ruler shrinks
Rung 2: the same ruler on a jagged coast; the length keeps climbing and the visitor predicts the next value before it appears
Rung 3: build a Koch coast step by step and watch each stage multiply the length by four thirds while the ruler shrinks by a third
Rung 4: the live log-log chart appears and the visitor drags a fitted line through the points to read the slope
Rung 5: turn the slope into a dimension and compare the circle (1), the Koch coast (about 1.26), and a seeded random coast whose roughness the visitor guesses first
Rung 6: a 'zoom out, zoom in' toggle shows a real quoted example (Great Britain at two ruler sizes) with the figures labelled as quoted, not measured here
checkQuestions: If shrinking the ruler by half makes a coast's length grow by about 20 percent, is the coast smoother or rougher than the Koch coast?
Why does a circle's measured length stop changing while a jagged coast's does not?
Why is a log-log chart, not an ordinary chart, the right one here?
Can a curve have dimension 1.5? What would that say about it?

research.summary: The coastline paradox is documented in an encyclopedia article and several explainers: Great Britain measured with 100 km units is about 2,800 km and with 50 km units about 3,400 km. The ruler-length versus measured-length chart on log-log axes is described as a straight line whose slope gives the fractal dimension, which is between 1 and 2 for coastlines, and the Koch curve has dimension ln 4 / ln 3 (about 1.2619) with length growing by 4/3 at each stage. Richardson and Mandelbrot are the origin; one source quotes Mandelbrot's figure of about 1.25 for the west coast of Britain, which the page would only show as quoted. The model is exact for self-similar curves and only an approximation for real coasts, which the page must say.

sources.title: Coastline paradox (Wikipedia)
sources.snippet: Coastlines have no well-defined length; for Great Britain about 2,800 km with 100 km units and about 3,400 km with 50 km units; Richardson found shorter units give longer borders.
sources.note: Encyclopedia statement of the paradox and the two Britain figures.

sources.title: How long is the coastline of Britain? (Skeptophilia)
sources.snippet: Blog post repeating the 100 km and 50 km Britain figures and noting the finer ruler adds a meaningful amount to the total.
sources.note: Independent second result for the Britain figures. Another site quoted about 3,500 km for the 50 km step, so the page says 'about'.

sources.title: Coastline paradox (MathWorld)
sources.snippet: Finer rulers capture more inlets so the total keeps rising; a log-log plot of ruler size against measured length gives a line related to the fractal dimension, between 1 and 2 for coastlines.
sources.note: Straight-line log-log relation and the 1 to 2 range for coasts. Single result for the log-log claim, so it stays unconfirmed.

sources.title: Fractals (New England Complex Systems Institute)
sources.snippet: The Koch curve has infinite length, no area, and dimension ln 4 / ln 3, about 1.2619.
sources.note: Koch dimension. A course page quoting 1.231 disagreed with the formula and is not used.

sources.title: Dimension Between Integers: Can We Measure the Length of a Coastline? (HKUST Science Focus)
sources.snippet: Explains the Koch construction in which the length grows by a factor of 4/3 at each stage, giving unbounded length.
sources.note: Second independent source for the Koch length growth.

sources.title: What is the coastline paradox? (Live Science)
sources.snippet: Explainer: Mandelbrot's Science paper 'How long is the coast of Britain?' built on Richardson's data and tied the effect to fractal geometry.
sources.note: Origin story for the Mandelbrot paper title.

sources.title: The length of a coastline (rspatial.org case study)
sources.snippet: A spatial-analysis tutorial reporting Mandelbrot's dimension of about 1.25 for the west coast of Britain and a student fit near 1.15 using modern data.
sources.note: Source for the 1.25 figure; only this one result, so it is shown as quoted.

sources.title: How long is a coastline (blog post)
sources.snippet: Blog listing dimensions for several coasts, such as Australia about 1.13 and Norway about 1.52, with a schematic chart.
sources.note: Not cross-checked against Richardson or Mandelbrot tables; these per-country figures are not used.

facts.claim: Measuring the coast of Great Britain with 100 km units gives about 2,800 km and with 50 km units about 3,400 km; the coastline has no well-defined length.
The Koch curve has dimension ln 4 / ln 3, about 1.2619, and its length grows by a factor of 4/3 at each stage so it is unbounded.
On log-log axes, measured length against ruler size lies near a straight line for a coastline, and the fractal dimension of a coast is between 1 and 2.

A coastline does not have a single well-defined length; the measured value depends on the ruler, and a smaller ruler gives a longer result (Richardson, then Mandelbrot's 1967 paper 'How long is the coast of Britain?').
Mandelbrot reported a dimension of about 1.25 for the west coast of Britain. Single result; show as 'as of 2026-10-14, per a spatial-analysis tutorial' or omit.

inspirations: Mandelbrot's 'How long is the coast of Britain?'

design.coreLoop: Shrink the ruler, predict the next length, see it, then watch a chart point appear. The next rung asks the visitor to fit the line and read the slope; a check question confirms the idea before the next curve.
sophisticationHooks: A correct divider walk (compass steps along the curve, each step a circle-curve intersection) so the ruler really walks the coast rather than being faked
Live log-log chart with a draggable fit line and a printed slope and dimension, rounded to the precision the data supports
Seeded random coasts with hidden roughness for a guess-the-dimension round with the answer revealed by measurement
An honesty panel: real coasts are only roughly self-similar over a limited range of ruler sizes, and the model is exact only for the built curves
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: Koch, circle and seeded midpoint-displacement coasts generated in the browser, divider-walk length function with unit tests, ruler slider, log-log chart with fit, 6 rungs, 4 check questions, explainer, and quoted Britain figures. Cut: real map data, country comparisons, user-drawn coasts (maybe a draw-your-own rung if time allows).
risks: Per-country dimensions (Australia, Norway, Portugal) came from one unreliable blog and are excluded; the Britain west-coast 1.25 figure is verified:false and must be shown as quoted or dropped.
Sketchplanations quoted about 3,500 km for the 50 km step against 3,400 km elsewhere, so the page says 'about' and cites the encyclopedia and one more source.
A course page gave the Koch dimension as 1.231; the formula ln4/ln3 = 1.2619 is used and the build should assert it in a test.
Looks like a fractal-pretty-picture page: the lesson must keep the chart and the slope reading central.
The coastline model is idealised; a real coast is not self-similar at every scale, and the page must say so.
The log-log straight-line claim rests on one search result (verified:false); the page demonstrates it with its own generated curves and labels the real-coast version as reported.
